title: Voltage drop from the intake, refined

interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is the total from the origin cross the 11.50 V limit near 60 m, when you drag the heater circuit's length. That total is the submain's 5.77 V plus the heater circuit's own drop.
interactive.title: The volts lost from the intake
interactive.whatAmILookingAt:
Eleven screens on voltage drop from the origin to the load, with Back and Continue. Screen 1, Do you still have it?: “A supply is given as 395 V. A submain feeding a second board has a calculated voltage drop of 10 V, and a radial power circuit from that board 9.8 V. Does the circuit comply?” The example is three-phase throughout, so it is judged on the three-phase voltage.[^16] Three choices, in this order: “No: 19.8 V is over 5% of 395 V, 19.75 V”; “Yes: 19.8 V is inside 5% of 400 V, 20.00 V”; “Yes: the radial's 9.8 V is inside the limit on its own”. Right is the first. It gives “Still there.” and the working: 10 + 9.8 = 19.8 V. It is three-phase throughout, so there is no ÷ √3. 395 × 0.05 = 19.75 V, so it does not comply.[^1] Then a line on each slip. Two buttons follow. Refresh the why goes on to screen 2, and Skip to the practice goes straight to screen 8. Wrong, the second: with 395 V given, take 5% of 395 V.[^2] BS 7671's Table 4Ab takes the nominal voltage, so the given voltage is the stricter test here.[^59] Wrong, the third: the limit covers every drop from the intake, the submain's 10 V too.[^3] Either way, the right working follows and the lesson goes on to screen 2. Read: 10 + 9.8 = 19.8 V. That is over 5% of the given 395 V, 19.75 V, so it does not comply.

Screen 2, What it is for. The cable's resistance uses up some of the supply's voltage on the way. The load gets what is left. The rule is VD = mV/A/m × Ib × L ÷ 1000.[^5] mV/A/m is the millivolts dropped for every ampere for every metre.[^4] On a public supply, Table 4Ab sets the limits. Lighting may drop up to 3%: 6.9 V single-phase and 12 V three-phase.[^6] Other circuits may drop up to 5%: 11.5 V and 20 V.[^7] The limit runs from the origin to the most distant point of the circuit.[^8] BS 7671 takes the percentages of the nominal voltage.[^59] In your assessments, take them of the supply voltage when one is given.[^2] That is the stricter test when the supply is below nominal. In red, if it is skipped or worked on one cable only: the load runs on less than it was designed for. A heater's power falls with the square of its voltage.[^9] A motor draws more current to keep its torque.[^10] A 3 kW heater on 85 m of 1.5 mm² drops 32.14 V.[^11] That is nearly three times the 11.50 V allowed.[^7] Read: work each drop as mV/A/m × Ib × L ÷ 1000. Keep the total from the origin to the far end within 3% for lighting or 5% for other circuits.

Screen 3, The why: the drop from the origin. The picture runs left to right, with short labels: Origin, Submain, Board, Heater circuit, Heater. Under it is the voltage along the path. It steps down across the submain and slopes down along the heater circuit. A red band is shaded below 218.50 V, which is 230 V less the 11.50 V limit. This screen puts two examples together. A 10 V submain drop, taken as three-phase, feeds a board. From that board runs the single-phase 3 kW heater: 13.04 A in 6.0 mm², 7.3 mV/A/m (Table 4D1B, column 3).[^12] No supply voltage is given, so the origin is the nominal 230 V. The submain's drop is line to line. The heater circuit runs line to neutral, a √3 smaller. So the submain's drop is divided by √3 before adding:[^13] 10.00 ÷ √3 = 5.77 V. That leaves 224.23 V at the board. A slider, Heater circuit length, runs from 0 to 120 m in 5 m steps and opens at 85 m. Readouts: Heater circuit's drop (7.3 × 13.04 × length ÷ 1000). Total from the origin (5.77 V plus that). Limit, 11.50 V.[^7] At 85 m the heater circuit drops 8.09 V,[^14] inside the limit on its own. But the total is 13.86 V, over the limit, and the heater's 216.14 V sits in the red band. At 60 m: 5.71 V, total 11.48 V, inside. At 65 m: 6.19 V, total 11.96 V, over. So the total crosses the limit near 60 m. The heater circuit alone stays inside it all the way to 120 m (11.42 V). The note under it says why. The heater gets what is left of the origin's voltage after every cable it is fed through.[^15] So the drops add.[^3] Read: at 85 m the heater circuit drops 8.09 V. With the submain's 5.77 V the total is 13.86 V, over 11.50 V. The total reaches the limit near 60 m.

Screen 4, Check: “A three-phase motor circuit has a calculated voltage drop of 7.2 V. Its board is fed by a three-phase submain with a calculated drop of 9.0 V. No supply voltage is given. What is the total, and does it comply?” Choices: “12.40 V: the submain's drop ÷ √3 first, so it complies”; “16.20 V, inside 20.00 V: it complies”; “16.20 V, over 11.50 V: it does not comply”. Right is the second: 7.2 + 9.0 = 16.20 V. It is three-phase all the way, so it is judged against 5% of 400 V.[^16] That is 20.00 V.[^7] Wrong, 12.40 V (9.0 ÷ √3 = 5.20 V, then 7.2 + 5.20): the ÷ √3 is for a three-phase submain feeding a single-phase circuit.[^13] This load is three-phase. Wrong, 11.50 V: that is 5% of 230 V. A three-phase circuit takes 5% of the three-phase voltage.[^16] Read: 7.2 + 9.0 = 16.20 V, inside 20.00 V.

Screen 5, Worked example, a line at each press. The words ask him to work each step first, then press Show the next step. The job: a 3 kW heater, 70 °C thermoplastic singles, 35 °C, Reference Method B, 85 m.[^17] Ib = 3000 ÷ 230 = 13.04 A. In is 16 A.[^60] Ca is 0.94.[^18] It ≥ 16 ÷ 0.94 = 17.02 A.[^61] 1.5 mm² is rated 17.5 A.[^62] VD = 29 × 13.04 × 85 ÷ 1000 = 32.14 V,[^11] over 11.50 V. Rounded to one place, 32.14 V is 32.1 V. Next, chase the volt drop: a bigger CSA, and the sum again, until it complies.[^19] The most mV/A/m that can pass at 85 m is 11.50 × 1000 ÷ (13.04 × 85) = 10.37, rounded down. 4.0 mm² is 11 mV/A/m (Table 4D1B, column 3).[^20] That is over it: 11 × 13.04 × 85 ÷ 1000 = 12.19 V, a fail. 6.0 mm² is 7.3 mV/A/m.[^12] 7.3 × 13.04 × 85 ÷ 1000 = 8.09 V, a pass.[^14] The last line: the 6.0 mm² carries just 13.04 A.[^21] Table 4D1A rates it at 41 A.[^22] Read: 1.5 mm² (32.14 V) and 4.0 mm² (12.19 V) fail. 6.0 mm² (8.09 V) passes. The most that can pass is 10.37 mV/A/m.

Screen 6, The why, refined: a lightly loaded cable. The opening text: the tables' mV/A/m assume the conductor is at its maximum operating temperature, 70 °C or 90 °C. It reaches that only at full load.[^23] Current heats a conductor, which raises its resistance and so the drop.[^24] At lower loads its temperature and resistance are lower.[^25] Ct corrects the drop for this. The picture uses the same heater, 13.04 A on 85 m. A named choice, Cable, offers 1.5 mm², 4.0 mm² and 6.0 mm², and opens on 6.0 mm². A switch, Apply Ct, opens off. A bar shows Ib as a share of It. Two bars in volts show the drop (red when over) and the 11.50 V limit. Under it, as a fraction on two lines: Ct = (230 + tp − (Ca² Cg² − Ib²/It²)(tp − 30)) ÷ (230 + tp).[^26] tp is the conductor's maximum operating temperature: 70 °C for PVC (thermoplastic), 90 °C for XLPE.[^27] Ca is the ambient temperature factor.[^28] It is the tabulated current rating.[^29] One way to picture Ib²/It²: heat goes with the square of the current. So 13.04 A in a cable rated 41 A makes about a tenth of its full-load heat. Here tp is 70 °C, Ca 0.94 (0.94² = 0.8836) and Cg 1. Readouts: Ib ÷ It, Ct and Drop. Each cable's working is in figures l5.ct.15, l5.ct.4 and l5.ct.6. 1.5 mm²: 29 mV/A/m, It 17.5 A (Table 4D1A, column 4).[^30] Ct 0.96 gives 30.85 V. Near its rating, a cable gains little. 4.0 mm²: 11 mV/A/m, It 32 A.[^31] (13.04 ÷ 32)² = 0.1661. 0.8836 − 0.1661 = 0.7175. × 40 = 28.70. (300 − 28.70) ÷ 300 = 0.9043, so Ct is 0.90. 12.19 × 0.90 = 10.97 V, inside. 6.0 mm²: 7.3 mV/A/m, It 41 A.[^32] Ct 0.90 gives 7.28 V. The moment to see: switch Ct on with 4.0 mm², and its bar falls under the limit. With Ct, a smaller CSA than 6.0 mm² may pass.[^33] A box headed Debated says to check this formula against Appendix 4 in your copy before relying on it.[^26] Some read it as counting only the ambient temperature and grouping factors,[^34] so Ci is left out here. Ct earns its keep where Ib is well below It and few correction factors apply.[^35] In one example, with a grouping factor of 0.78 and nothing else, Ct was only about 0.99.[^36] Read: in 4.0 mm² the heater circuit drops 12.19 V, over 11.50 V. With Ct 0.90 it drops 10.97 V, inside.

Screen 7, The why, refined: a known power factor. From 25 mm² up, the tables give r, x and z.[^37] They give them separately for the larger cables.[^38] With no known power factor, z is acceptable.[^39] With one, use r and x.[^40] The picture: the r drop is an arrow along the current. The x drop runs a quarter-cycle ahead of it, at right angles. z joins their ends, drawn from r and x: √(1.60² + 0.27²) = 1.62. The table's z, 1.65, is not exactly √(r² + x²), and a tick on the voltage line marks it. The load's voltage is a line at the angle φ from the current, with each drop's shadow along it. A slider, Power factor, runs from 0.50 to 1.00 in steps of 0.05 and opens at 0.80, the showroom motor's. The cable is 25 mm² 90 °C singles in conduit, three-phase: r 1.60, x 0.27, z 1.65 mV/A/m (Table 4E1B).[^41] Readouts: sin φ = √(1 − cos² φ).[^42] Drop per amp per metre, r × cos φ + x × sin φ.[^43] z, 1.65. At 1.00 the drop is 1.60. At 0.80: 1.60 × 0.8 + 0.27 × 0.6 = 1.28 + 0.16 = 1.44 mV/A/m, about 13% under z. At 0.50 (sin φ 0.87): 0.80 + 0.23 = 1.03. Why: the r drop is in step with the current, and the x drop is a quarter-cycle ahead. So only their parts along the load's voltage take away from its size. Taking z as if all of it lay along the voltage may give a drop higher than the actual one.[^44] r and x give an accurate figure for loads with a large inductive element.[^45] So a circuit may conform without being upsized.[^46] This lesson does not combine Ct with r and x. Read: at power factor 0.8, 1.60 × 0.8 + 0.27 × 0.6 = 1.44 mV/A/m, against z's 1.65.

Screen 8, Section A, question 1 (g). It shows the scenario panel, and parts (a) to (f) carried forward. The givens, all assumed here: the motor is fed from DBP2, about 11.4 m along the walls on plan. That is approximate: a real design adds the vertical runs. DBP2 to the starter is 2.5 mm² 90 °C thermosetting singles in conduit, one three-phase circuit, 16 mV/A/m (Table 4E1B, column 6).[^47] Starter to motor is part (f)'s six 1.5 mm² singles, 3.0 m. That length is a practice value: measure the real run. They are 31 mV/A/m for two cables single-phase (column 3).[^48] The DBP2 submain's three-phase drop is 4.00 V, a practice value. The leg: in delta running, the windings are three single-phase loads.[^49] Each is fed through two of the six conductors, one at each end.[^50] Each conductor carries the winding current, 13.33 A (part b). We take the leg's drop as 31 × 13.33 × 3.0 ÷ 1000, line to line, and add it to the rest. That reading is ours, not BS 7671's, and it is debated. Some multiply by √3 as well,[^51] which gives 2.15 V here. “(g) Determine the actual voltage drop of the motor circuit, from the intake to the motor.” A typed answer (part 1g): 16 × 23.08 × 11.4 ÷ 1000 = 4.21 V. 31 × 13.33 × 3.0 ÷ 1000 = 1.24 V. 4.00 + 4.21 + 1.24 = 9.45 V, on practice values. That is inside 5% of 400 V, 20.00 V:[^7] 2.36%. There is no ÷ √3, because the motor is three-phase.[^16] Two other answers are accepted, each with its own line. 10.36 V is the other reading of the leg. The line current, 31 × 23.08 × 3.0 ÷ 1000, gives the same 2.15 V, though each conductor carries the winding current.[^52] 9.15 V is the drop with Ct. Slips: 5.45 V leaves out the submain.[^3] 8.21 V leaves out the leg, and every length of the run counts. 7.76 V divides the submain's drop by √3 (2.31 V), which is for a single-phase circuit.[^13] After two misses, the working shows. Then a fold, Refined with Ct (working: l5.A.1g.ct). The 2.5 mm² cable carries 23.08 A of its 28 A (Table 4E1A, column 5).[^53] Take tp as 90 °C, Ca as 1.00, a practice value, and Cg as 1. Then Ct is 0.94, giving 3.96 V. The leg has Cg 0.80 and It 20 A.[^54] Its Ct is 0.96, giving 1.19 V. In all that is 9.15 V. It is not needed, since 9.45 V passes. The power factor comes in only from 25 mm² up, so it is left out here.[^37] Read: 4.00 + 4.21 + 1.24 = 9.45 V, on practice values. That is inside 20.00 V.

Screen 9, Section B: “Explain why a cable carrying well under its rating drops less voltage than Appendix 4's mV/A/m gives, and how a designer can take credit for it.” A written answer, marked against five points. Any three make a full answer. He gets one more go, then the model answer.

Screen 10, Section A, changed numbers: “A single-phase power circuit, 32 m of 1.5 mm² 90 °C singles in conduit (31 mV/A/m), Ib 9 A, is fed from a sub-board whose three-phase submain drops 7.5 V. No supply voltage is given. Determine the total voltage drop from the origin.”[^48] A typed answer: 31 × 9 × 32 ÷ 1000 = 8.93 V. 7.5 ÷ √3 = 4.33 V.[^13] 4.33 + 8.93 = 13.26 V, over 11.50 V. It fails, though the circuit alone would pass. 13.27 V is accepted too: that takes √3 as 1.73.[^55] Slips: 16.43 V adds the submain's drop with no ÷ √3. 21.92 V multiplies it by √3 (7.5 × √3 = 12.99 V). 8.93 V leaves the submain out.[^3] Read: 8.93 V. 7.5 ÷ √3 = 4.33 V. 4.33 + 8.93 = 13.26 V, over 11.50 V.

Screen 11, Keep this: the summary card, then Finish the lesson. The line under screens 3 to 8 and 10 says that practice values are marked, and that each line is worked from the rounded figures before it.
interactive.ignores: The path on screen 3 is drawn as one straight run with two cables. A real installation branches, and each circuit is checked to its own far end. The submain and the heater are two separate examples put together, not one job. The heater's current is held at 13.04 A whatever the length, because the drop rule takes Ib as fixed. A real heater draws a little less on a lower voltage. On screen 6 the cable's temperature is shown only as Ib's share of It, not in degrees. On screen 7 the shadows of the r and x drops along the voltage are the usual close approximation. They are very near the exact figure while the drop is small beside the supply voltage.

explain.text:
Voltage drop is the voltage the cables use up on the way to the load. The load gets what is left. Work it as mV/A/m × Ib × L ÷ 1000.[^5] mV/A/m is the millivolts dropped for every ampere of design current, for every metre of conductor.[^4] On a public supply, lighting may drop up to 3% of the supply.[^6] Other circuits may drop up to 5%.[^7] BS 7671 takes those percentages of the nominal voltage.[^59] In your assessments, take them of the supply voltage when one is given.[^2] That is the stricter test when the given voltage is lower.

The limit runs from the origin of the installation to the most distant point of the circuit.[^8] That is because the load gets what is left of the origin's voltage after every cable it is fed through. So add the submain's drop to the final circuit's.[^15] A final circuit that passes on its own can still fail. Take a 395 V supply, three-phase throughout, with 10 V lost in the submain and 9.8 V in the circuit. That makes 19.8 V, over the 19.75 V allowed.[^1] A three-phase submain's drop is a line-to-line figure. A single-phase circuit runs line to neutral, a √3 smaller. So where a three-phase submain feeds a single-phase circuit, divide its drop by √3 before adding.[^13] Where the load is three-phase too, keep every drop three-phase. Judge the total against 3% or 5% of the three-phase voltage.[^16]

Two refinements can bring a narrow fail inside the limit. First, the tables' mV/A/m assume the conductor is at its maximum operating temperature. It reaches that only at full load.[^23] Current heats a conductor, and a hotter conductor has more resistance.[^24] So a cable carrying well under its rating runs cooler and drops less.[^25] A factor, [[Ct]], corrects the drop for this. Take a 3 kW heater cable sized up to 6.0 mm² for voltage drop. It carries just 13.04 A.[^21] Its rating is 41 A.[^22] So it drops less than the table's 8.09 V.[^57] With Ct, the smaller 4.0 mm² may pass.[^33] Second, from 25 mm² up the tables give r, x and z.[^37] With a known power factor, the r drop is in step with the current. The x drop runs a quarter of a cycle ahead of it. So only their parts along the load's voltage take away from it: (mV/A/m)r × cos φ + (mV/A/m)x × sin φ.[^43] Using z alone may give a drop higher than the actual one.[^44] This is a simplification. It stays very close to the exact figure while the drop is small beside the supply voltage.

**Add every drop from the intake to the far end. Judge the total against 3% or 5%. In your assessments, take the percentage of the voltage given. BS 7671 takes it of the nominal voltage. Where the total fails narrowly, Ct on a lightly loaded cable may show that it passes. So may r and x, with a known power factor.**

analogy.text: Think of a ship's fresh-water main. The pressure at a shower on the far deck is the pump's pressure less what is lost in every length of pipe on the way, the ring main as well as the branch. A branch that loses little on its own can still leave too little at the shower. The ring main has already taken its share. So you judge the loss from the pump, not from the branch's own valve.
analogy.breaks: A pipe's loss climbs faster than its flow, while a cable's drop is in proportion to its current. An AC cable's reactance also drops voltage out of step with the current. A pipe has nothing like that, so the r and x refinement has no water version.

practice.text:
- Work out Ib at the voltage given, as in lesson 1. Then work each cable's drop: mV/A/m × Ib × L ÷ 1000.[^5] Take mV/A/m from the Appendix 4 voltage-drop table for that cable and how it is installed.[^58]
- Add every drop from the intake to the end of the circuit.[^3] That means the submain's drop as well as the final circuit's.[^15] Count every length of the run, not just the main routes.
- A three-phase submain feeding a single-phase circuit: divide the submain's drop by √3 before adding.[^13] A three-phase load: keep every drop three-phase.[^16]
- On a public supply, judge the total against 3% for lighting.[^6] For other circuits, judge it against 5%.[^7] In your assessments, take the percentage of the voltage given.[^2] Where none is given, take the nominal 230 V or 400 V. BS 7671 takes it of the nominal voltage.[^59] So the assessment test is stricter when the given voltage is lower.
- Fails? Chase it with a bigger CSA, and work the sum again until it complies.[^19] Then, for a cable carrying well under its rating, try Ct.[^35] At 25 mm² and over, with a known power factor, use r and x.[^40]

**Rule of thumb:** take the limit, less any submain's drop. Multiply it by 1000 and divide by Ib × L. That is the most mV/A/m that can pass. The first cable under it is the one to try. Ct earns most where Ib is well below It and few correction factors apply.[^35] In one example, with a grouping factor of 0.78 and nothing else, Ct was only about 0.99.[^36]

**Worked example:** the showroom motor, part 1(g). The DBP2 submain's 4.00 V and the 3.0 m leg are practice values. DBP2 to the starter is 2.5 mm² (Table 4E1B, column 6): 16 × 23.08 × 11.4 ÷ 1000 = 4.21 V.[^47] The leg is 1.5 mm² (column 3), worked at the winding current: 31 × 13.33 × 3.0 ÷ 1000 = 1.24 V.[^48] This step is debated: some multiply by √3 as well.[^51] The total is 4.00 + 4.21 + 1.24 = 9.45 V, inside 5% of 400 V, 20.00 V.[^7] There is no ÷ √3, since the motor is three-phase.[^16]

**Common mistakes**
- Checking the final circuit on its own. The limit covers every drop from the intake.[^3]
- Taking 5% of 400 V when the supply is given as 395 V.[^1] In your assessments, take the voltage given.[^2]
- Dividing by √3 when the load is three-phase.[^16]
- Using z with a known power factor on 25 mm² and over. It may overstate the drop.[^44]
- Taking the Ct formula's factors as settled. The one here uses Ca and Cg, not Ci.[^34] Check it against Appendix 4 in your copy.

b1.q: Explain why a cable carrying well under its rating drops less voltage than Appendix 4's mV/A/m gives, and how a designer can take credit for it.

points.text: Appendix 4's mV/A/m values are for the conductor at its maximum operating temperature, 70 °C or 90 °C. It reaches that only at full load.
points.cite: TiSoft, voltage drop according to BS 7671, in research

points.text: Current heats a conductor, and a hotter conductor has more resistance, so a larger voltage drop.
A cable carrying well below its rating, with Ib well under It, runs cooler. So its resistance and its drop are lower than the table gives.
The correction factor Ct multiplies the tabulated drop. It is worked from Ib and It, the conductor's maximum temperature, and the ambient and grouping factors.
points.cite: Slides p.43; the Ct formula as quoted on myElectrical and defined by TiSoft, in research

points.text: It can let a smaller cable pass. For example, a 3 kW heater in 4.0 mm² drops 12.19 V by the table and 10.97 V with Ct, against 11.50 V. You do not need the example to score this point.
points.cite: Slides p.42, 43; Tables 4D1A and 4D1B, your copy p.448, 449

b1.model: Appendix 4's mV/A/m values assume the conductor is at its maximum operating temperature, 70 °C or 90 °C. It reaches that only when it carries its full load. Current heats a conductor, and a hotter conductor has more resistance, so more drop. A cable carrying well under its rating, Ib well below It, runs cooler. So its resistance and its drop are lower than the table says. The designer takes credit with the factor Ct, which multiplies the tabulated drop. Ct is worked from Ib and It, the maximum operating temperature, and the ambient and grouping factors. It can let a smaller cable pass. A 3 kW heater in 4.0 mm² drops 12.19 V by the table but 10.97 V with Ct, inside the 11.50 V limit.

summary.title: Voltage drop from the intake, refined
summary.for: Enough voltage must reach the load. Keep the drop from the origin to the far end of the circuit within 3% for lighting or 5% for other circuits, on a public supply. BS 7671 takes the percentage of the nominal voltage. In your assessments, take it of the voltage given.
summary.rule:
VD = mV/A/m × Ib × L ÷ 1000
Total = submain + final circuit, from the intake
3-phase submain, 1-phase circuit: submain ÷ √3
Limit, public supply: lighting 3% (6.9 V 1-ph, 12 V 3-ph); others 5% (11.5 V, 20 V)
BS 7671: % of the nominal voltage. Assessments: % of the voltage given
Ct = (230 + tp − (Ca² Cg² − Ib²/It²)(tp − 30)) ÷ (230 + tp)
25 mm² and up, power factor known: r × cos φ + x × sin φ

Fails? Chase it with a bigger CSA, then try Ct on the size below it.
A three-phase load keeps every drop three-phase.
Check the Ct formula against Appendix 4 in your copy before you rely on it.

traps.text: Checking the final circuit on its own. The limit covers every drop from the intake to the end of the circuit.
traps.cite: Project guide p.6; formula sheet step 7

traps.text: Taking 5% of 400 V when the supply is given as 395 V. In your assessments the limit is then 19.75 V, not 20 V. BS 7671 itself takes the nominal voltage.
traps.cite: Slides p.40, 41; NAPIT, how to determine voltage drop limits, in research

traps.text: Dividing by √3 when the load is three-phase. The ÷ √3 is for a three-phase submain feeding a single-phase circuit.
Using z on 25 mm² and over when the power factor is known. It may overstate the drop.

traps.text: Leaving a cable chased up for voltage drop at its tabulated drop. It runs cooler, and with Ct a smaller cable may pass.
